items.title: Michael White interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 10, 2025
items.q: He sounds like Chester Zardis and Bill Johnson and Al Morgan you know and all these people.

ctx.x: I think you started to answer my question because I think it’s probably harder to teach this music. Because try to think of the last time you saw a New Orleans style jazz group play with music stands in front of them. And I don’t think the music lends itself to being codified, to have all those scales and it’s such a personal thing, and all those connections, those community connections you just mentioned that are part and the reason for the music. How do you teach that? And if someone can’t teach it they decide…

Well yeah, and also I mean just the fact that a lot of later generation people, you know, you like the music of your generation or whatever, and a lot of people just didn’t respect it ‘cause it was old, or they didn’t respect it because they didn’t think it was hip. You know they didn’t use as many scales and altered things and it wasn’t, in general, as fast and technical. You know it presented a different kind of challenge. It wasn’t something that you could sit down and say analyze and say this is this scale…

Orleans and she sounds more like the authentic trombone style than most people in New Orleans today you know. There’s a guy, a young guy from Canada, Toronto, who moved to New Orleans and he plays bass and he sounds like the old bass players. He sounds like Chester Zardis and Bill Johnson and Al Morgan you know and all these people. But he’s very creative you know. And so that’s – the way I feel about the music, I’m finding that some of these younger people all over the world feel the same way that you can play…
